source.title: Asymptotics of Ridge Regression in Convolutional Models
source.authors: Mojtaba Sahraee-Ardakan; Tung Mai; Anup B. Rao; Ryan A. Rossi; Sundeep Rangan; Alyson K. Fletcher

record.tranche_reason: It tests double descent in convolutional ridge regression using asymptotic analysis and simulations, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study varies the model dimension and reports normalized estimation error curves. It does not vary epochs or training-sample count. Cited results about double descent are not recorded as rows. The reported metric is estimation error, not an explicitly described held-out test-set error.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates estimation error of convolutional ridge regression (deconvolution) as the parameter count nx grows with ny=500 fixed. The authors state the curve shows double descent with a peak at δ=1. This is a new, non-deep model class bearing on V4, so T3 fits better than T2. It does not re-run the original deep-network method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the asymptotic MSE is a scalar integral depending on the signal's spectral density, which the AR(1) experiments confirm. Double descent appears versus δ=ny/nx with a peak at δ=1, and regularization lowers error near the threshold.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes ridge estimation in convolutional linear inverse problems, using asymptotic theory and synthetic-data experiments; it does not reproduce the original deep-network training and test-error procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported error curves vary with ridge regularization λ and with the signal process; the AR(1) cases differ from the i.i.d. case, while matched-variance Gaussian and uniform AR(1) process noise give nearly indistinguishable plots.

fits_no_version.finding: Asymptotic ridge error in convolutional models depends on the signal only through its spectral density. AR(1) signals give error-vs-δ curves very different from i.i.d. signals, while uniform and Gaussian AR(1) noise with matched variance give near-identical curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The shape of the double-descent curve in linear deconvolution is governed by the input's spectral density, not its marginal distribution.

record.problems: The empirical results are presented in figures without extractable numerical curve values or uncertainty estimates. The experiment varies nx with ny fixed and reports estimation error, not an explicitly specified held-out test-set measure.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result meeting the row criteria was left out. References to double-descent findings from other studies were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No deep networks. The deep-network double descent is cited only as motivation.
ny is fixed at 500 and only nx is varied. Sample-wise non-monotonicity is implied by the δ-only theory but not directly tested.
Only convolutional linear ridge regression on synthetic data is tested, and the measure is estimation error rather than held-out prediction risk.
Whether label noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, and whether optimally tuned λ removes the peak are not tested. Only three unstated λ values are shown.

missing.what: Theoretical result (Remark 3, Corollary 1) that for i.i.d. priors the convolutional ridge error vs δ equals the ordinary ridge double-descent curve, with a closed-form error formula as a function of λ and δ. This is analytic support for V4/V6 beyond the simulation rows.

record.verdict_notes: Error depends only on δ in theory, so the same curves would imply sample-wise non-monotonicity (V3) in this linear setting. The experiment, however, only varies nx. The reader's V6 limits_scope label rested on untested parts, which is not a valid ground; I replaced it with a narrow supports label and listed the untested parts. Tranche changed from T2 to T3. Regarding the measure: in this isotropic setup, normalized estimation error tracks excess prediction risk but is not explicitly a test-set error.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies dimension in convolutional linear ridge regression, not model size in deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The number of measurements is fixed at ny=500 in the described experiments; the study does not increase training-sample count near interpolation.
The tested model class is convolutional linear ridge regression, not all model classes; the study reports estimation error rather than explicitly held-out test risk.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The experiments vary ridge regularization and discuss its effect near interpolation. They do not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.condition: Convolutional ridge regression with i.i.d. complex normal or AR(1) (uniform or Gaussian process noise) signal rows, T=256, ny=500
relationships.reason: Authors state that error decreases again past the interpolation threshold δ=1 (nx=ny), with theory matching simulation (r1–r9). This rests on figures; no numbers are given.
relationships.display_finding: Error decreased again beyond δ=1, where nx=ny, with theoretical predictions matching simulations.

relationships.condition: Three unstated ridge λ values, i.i.d. Gaussian features (Figure 1)
relationships.reason: The text says regularization pulls estimation error down near the interpolation threshold, consistent with the peak being regularization-dependent (r1–r3). Whether optimal λ removes the peak is untested.
relationships.display_finding: Regularization reduced estimation error near the interpolation threshold across the three tested ridge settings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Convolutional ridge regression on the tested i.i.d. and AR(1) signal settings
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a double-descent estimation-error curve as dimension changes, with a peak at the stated interpolation threshold δ=1; the curves are shown in rows r1–r9.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Regularization is reported to lower error near interpolation, but the study does not test optimal tuning or establish that regularization removes the peak; rows r1–r9 show the plotted λ conditions.
